query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures in oxidizing environments, selective oxidation of reactive elements (notably Al and Cr) at the grain boundaries in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA leads to the formation of brittle oxide phases that weaken intergranular cohesion, thereby governing degradation and predisposing the alloy to catastrophic failure. In contrast, reducing or inert atmospheres suppress this grain‐boundary oxidation, delaying degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous FCC matrix and relatively uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Switch the high-temperature exposure gas from an oxidizing (oxygen-rich) environment to a reducing or inert environment while maintaining temperature and exposure time.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–1050 °C) for durations sufficient to allow diffusion-driven elemental segregation and oxide precipitation in atmospheres that are either strongly oxidizing or reducing.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries where oxidation-induced segregation of reactive elements forms brittle oxide precipitates that disrupt the cohesive strength of the microstructural network.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, diffusive processes promote the segregation of Al and Cr to grain boundaries where, in oxidizing atmospheres, they form brittle, adherent oxide phases. These phases act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, undermining intergranular bonding and ultimately leading to catastrophic failure under mechanical loading. Under reducing conditions, this selective oxidation is suppressed, resulting in lower oxide buildup and enhanced ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline state, samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will show increased grain-boundary oxidation (e.g., thicker, continuous brittle oxide films) accompanied by reduced ductility and premature catastrophic failure under stress. In reducing conditions, a significant reduction in grain-boundary oxide formation is expected, preserving the mechanical integrity and delaying failure.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated, additively manufactured alloy featuring a uniform FCC matrix with no pre-existing, concentrated grain-boundary oxides or embrittling phases.
generation.boundary: Observations are applicable within the temperature range of 700–1050 °C, where diffusion and oxidation processes are prominent, and in gas environments ranging from strongly oxidizing (oxygen-rich) to reducing (e.g., hydrogen-rich or inert gas conditions).
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of each reactive element (Al, Cr, Ti) to the oxidation process and the influence of any microstructural anisotropies introduced by additive manufacturing remain uncertain and require further detailed study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical sets of the alloy samples and expose them at selected temperatures (e.g., 800, 900, and 1000 °C) for a fixed duration in both oxidizing (oxygen-rich) and reducing (inert or hydrogen-rich) atmospheres. After exposure, conduct microstructural analysis using SEM/TEM to characterize grain-boundary oxide thickness/distribution and perform mechanical tests (tensile, fracture toughness) to assess failure behavior.
measurements: Grain-boundary oxide layer thickness and continuity (via TEM/SEM)
Elemental segregation profiles (using EDS or similar techniques)
Tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness
Crack initiation and propagation sites during mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exposed to oxidizing conditions do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in grain-boundary oxide formation or demonstrate degraded mechanical performance (e.g., lower ductility, earlier catastrophic failure) compared to those exposed in reducing conditions, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary oxidation governs degradation and catastrophic failure is falsified.

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [7] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ] This well‐established mechanism highlights the central role of brittle phase precipitation and element segregation at GBs in governing embrittlement in conventional alloys.

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
